Prompts add declarations of called functions, previously defined local variables and offset-to-string mappings; the outputs are then reassembled, with string constants restored and variables renamed. Training data come from 51,768 the-stack-dedup and 377 TheAlgorithms/C programs compiled with Emscripten. On 3,977 C files, the authors report 3.34% code inflation, 52.11% recompilability, 43.55% re-execution and 27.15% output consistency, compared with Wasm2c and Ghidra.

papers.title: Web2Code: A Large-scale Webpage-to-Code Dataset and Evaluation Framework for Multimodal LLMs
papers.description: Studies screenshot-to-HTML reconstruction through instruction tuning and two evaluation benchmarks. Web2Code combines generated webpages, refined WebSight and pix2code image/code pairs, and WebSRC-derived question answering. Models produce HTML from a webpage image and instruction; rendered output is compared visually, while a separate benchmark measures screenshot understanding.

papers.title: WorldCoder, a Model-Based LLM Agent: Building World Models by Writing Code and Interacting with the Environment
papers.description: WorldCoder learns executable Python transition and reward models from environment interactions and natural-language goals. It refines code against recorded experiences and an optimistic planning constraint, studying transfer and task solving in Sokoban, MiniGrid and ALFWorld.

papers.title: “Len or index or count, anything but v1”: Predicting Variable Names in Decompilation Output with Transfer Learning
papers.description: VarBERT suggests variable names for IDA Hex-Rays and Ghidra decompiler output with a BERT-style model pre-trained on 5.2M human-written C functions from Debian and fine-tuned on decompiled code; it also predicts whether each variable came from the developer or was introduced by the decompiler. The authors build VarCorpus from Gentoo C and C++ packages compiled for x86-64 at O0–O3, labeling decompiled variables from debug symbols. On per-function splits of O2 binaries, top-1 accuracy is 54.43% for IDA and 54.49% for Ghidra; on an IDA-O0 subset it reaches 50.70%, against 35.94% for DIRE and 38.00% for DIRTY.

papers.title: Asteria-Pro: Enhancing Deep-Learning Based Binary Code Similarity Detection by Incorporating Domain Knowledge
papers.description: Asteria-Pro adds domain-knowledge pre-filtration and re-ranking to Tree-LSTM-based binary code similarity detection. It evaluates firmware vulnerability search across diverse IoT hardware architectures.

papers.title: Binary Code Summarization: Benchmarking ChatGPT/GPT-4 and Other Large Language Models
papers.description: BinSum benchmarks LLMs on summarizing binary functions in natural language. The authors compile 44 GNU projects with GCC 7.5 for x86, x64, ARM and MIPS at -O0 to -O3, match 557,664 binary functions to developer comments as reference summaries, and present each function as raw bytes, assembly, IDA microcode or decompiled code with and without symbols. GPT-4, ChatGPT, Llama 2 and Code Llama receive prompts selected from 320 GPT-4-generated candidates, with the fine-tuned BinT5 as a baseline; outputs are scored by embedding similarity alongside BLEU, METEOR and ROUGE-L. Decompiled code is the most useful representation, and stripping symbols lowers the average similarity score from 0.449 to 0.202.

papers.title: BinaryInferno: A Semantic-Driven Approach to Field Inference for Binary Message Formats
papers.description: Infers partial binary-message formats from static message samples without instrumenting an executable. Specialized detectors recognize floats, timestamps, lengths, entropy boundaries and serialization patterns; a graph-based integration step reconciles their descriptions. Across samples from ten protocols, the authors report top-level field-boundary precision of 0.69, recall of 0.73 and false-positive rate of 0.04 for the 1,000-message setting without analyst priors.

papers.title: Combining Functional and Automata Synthesis to Discover Causal Reactive Programs
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (POPL 2023)
papers.description: AutumnSynth synthesizes a program in Autumn, a functional reactive language for Atari-style grid worlds, from a trace of observed frames and user actions such as clicks and arrow keys. Heuristic perception parses each frame into typed objects and tracking links them across time steps. The synthesizer then finds an update function for each observed change and searches for the event that triggers it. When no event over the observed state explains an update, automata synthesis invents latent state, such as counters or modes, using a SAT-based Sketch encoding or a faster heuristic. The authors introduce the 30-program Causal Inductive Synthesis Corpus (CISC), on which the heuristic variant synthesizes 27 programs. A slightly modified version synthesizes 21 of 27 games from the third-party EMPA grid-world corpus.

papers.title: Decompiling x86 Deep Neural Network Executables
papers.description: BTD (Bin to DNN) decompiles stripped 64-bit x86 executables emitted by deep-learning compilers into model specifications: operator types, network topology, dimensions and parameters. A learned classifier labels disassembled functions as DNN operators, Intel Pin dynamic analysis chains them, and taint-reduced, trace-based symbolic execution with per-operator patterns recovers dimensions and parameter layouts. The authors rebuild recovered models in PyTorch and recompile them to compare behaviour with the original executable.

papers.title: Extracting Protocol Format as State Machine via Controlled Static Loop Analysis
papers.description: The paper extracts protocol message formats from parser code by analyzing parsing loops as state machines. It evaluates format inference and the use of the extracted machines in protocol fuzzers.

papers.title: kTrans: Knowledge-Aware Transformer for Binary Code Embedding
papers.description: kTrans uses a knowledge-aware Transformer to embed binary code. It evaluates the embeddings through outlier detection and visualization, and on binary code similarity, function type recovery, and indirect call recognition.

papers.title: Lifting Network Protocol Implementation to Precise Format Specification with Security Applications
papers.description: NetLifter statically lifts source-available C protocol parsers into BNF-style message grammars and first-order constraints between packet fields. It analyzes annotated LLVM bitcode using abstract format graphs, localized path-sensitive analysis, unfolding and reordering. The resulting field boundaries, constraints and names can support packet generation and parser construction.

papers.title: Refining Decompiled C Code with Large Language Models
papers.description: The paper proposes a two-step hybrid LLM approach to refine IDA-Pro decompiled C code for recompilation. On popular C test cases, it reports a recompilation success rate above 75% with moderate effort.

papers.title: Revisiting Binary Code Similarity Analysis Using Interpretable Feature Engineering and Lessons Learned
papers.description: Builds BinKit, a reproducible cross-compilation benchmark of 243,128 binaries and 36,256,322 functions from 51 GNU packages, covering 1,352 combinations of eight architectures, nine GCC and Clang versions, five optimization levels, and PIE, LTO, no-inline and Obfuscator-LLVM options. TikNib, an interpretable baseline over simple presemantic function features, measures how compilers, options and architectures change those features. The authors report that a few basic features approach a deep-learning tool’s accuracy, that type features push AUC above 0.99, and trace failures to IDA Pro analysis errors, compiler back-end differences and architecture-specific code.

papers.title: XFL: Naming Functions in Binaries with Extreme Multi-label Learning
papers.description: XFL treats function naming in stripped binaries as extreme multi-label classification: names are split into tokens, and PfastreXML ranks which tokens from a vocabulary of frequent labels fit each function. Its DEXTER embedding combines static-analysis features built on angr’s VEX IR with call-graph and whole-binary context, and a separate language model orders predicted tokens into a name string. On 741,724 functions from 10,047 x86-64 C binaries in Debian packages, with a 1,024-label vocabulary, the authors report precision 0.835, recall 0.575 and F1 0.681, ahead of Punstrip, Debin and Nero in precision and F1.

papers.title: Augmenting Decompiler Output with Learned Variable Names and Types
papers.description: Introduces DIRTY, a Transformer model that recommends variable names and types from decompiled code and layout information, together with the DIRT corpus for training and evaluation.

papers.title: Automated Attack Synthesis by Extracting Finite State Machines from Protocol Specification Documents
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022
papers.description: Extracts protocol FSMs from RFC prose using technical word representations, zero-shot text mapping, and rules, then uses the extracted FSMs to synthesize attacks.

papers.title: Beyond the C: Retargetable Decompilation using Neural Machine Translation
papers.description: BTC (Beyond The C) treats decompilation as plain-text translation from compiler-emitted x86-64 assembly to source code. It uses byte-pair-encoding tokenizers trained separately on assembly and source, and a standard fairseq transformer. Function pairs are matched through the compiler's CFI and line directives rather than language-specific parsers, compiler plugins or lifters, so the same pipeline is retrained for Go, Fortran, OCaml and C. Training sets range from about 10,000 functions for small C, Go and Fortran corpora to 2 million C functions built from Debian packages. The best model, trained on the large C set, reaches a normalized average edit distance of 0.46 on held-out functions.

papers.title: Decomperson: How Humans Decompile and What We Can Learn From It
papers.description: Reframes manual reverse engineering as perfect decompilation: writing source that, compiled with the original toolchain and options, reproduces the target functions’ binary code exactly. The authors built Decomperson, a web editor that compiles, disassembles, tests and diffs each submission, and used it in Decompetition, a 24-hour Jeopardy-style competition in November 2020 with 23 unstripped challenge binaries written in C, C++, Go, Rust and Swift. Over 150 participants made more than 35,000 submissions, including over 300 perfect ones; all but one challenge was perfectly decompiled, and the recorded edit histories are analyzed to describe how humans decompile.

papers.title: DeepDi: Learning a Relational Graph Convolutional Network Model on Instructions for Fast and Accurate Disassembly
papers.description: DeepDi disassembles x86 and x64 binaries by decoding a superset of candidate instructions, linking them in an Instruction Flow Graph of forward, backward and overlap relations, and classifying true instructions with a Relational Graph Convolutional Network; heuristics and a small classifier then recover function entry points. On BAP corpora, LLVM 11 built with MSVC on Windows, and SPEC CPU2006 and CPU2017, the authors report accuracy comparable or superior to IDA Pro, Binary Ninja, Ghidra, Datalog Disassembly and XDA, robustness on Linn–Debray and Hikari obfuscated binaries, single-core CPU throughput of 146 KB/s (about twice IDA Pro) and GPU throughput of 24.5 MB/s (about 350 times IDA Pro).

papers.title: Elipmoc: Advanced Decompilation of Ethereum Smart Contracts
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA 2022)
papers.description: Elipmoc decompiles Ethereum Virtual Machine bytecode into a structured three-address intermediate representation for security analyses and reverse engineering. Built as an evolution of the Datalog-based Gigahorse decompiler, it adds transactional context sensitivity, path-sensitive inference of function arguments and returns with path merging, and fully context-sensitive reconstruction of private functions. On a uniform random sample of 5,000 unique mainnet contracts first deployed between April and September 2021, the authors report fully resolved operands for 99.5% of contracts versus 62.8% for Gigahorse, 67% more unique external-call signatures than Etherscan’s Panoramix, and over 5x faster decompilation.

papers.title: ExeBench: an ML-scale dataset of executable C functions
papers.description: ExeBench is a dataset, not a decompiler. It extracts C functions from GitHub and AnghaBench, makes them compilable by locating real headers and definitions or injecting synthetic ones, and generates input/output examples from function signatures with a C++ wrapper that runs each function. After exact deduplication the authors report 4,485,817 compilable and 687,843 executable functions, of which 124,612 have rich IO that a constant or identity implementation cannot pass; the paper also describes x86 and ARM assembly at O0, Os and Ofast for each row. Decompilation studies such as SLaDe and LLM4Decompile later used it to test whether decompiled functions re-execute correctly.

papers.title: Fingerprinting and analysis of Bluetooth devices with automata learning
papers.description: Learns Mealy-machine models of Bluetooth Low Energy implementations on physical peripherals by active automata learning. An nRF52840 central running SweynTooth-derived firmware sends abstract BLE inputs, with error handling, repeated queries and caching for lost packets and non-deterministic replies. The authors learn connection-procedure models of six devices and legacy-pairing models of three, and use model differences to fingerprint their SoCs.

papers.title: Fuzzware: Using Precise MMIO Modeling for Effective Firmware Fuzzing
papers.description: Rehosts monolithic ARM Cortex-M firmware for fuzzing, using locally scoped symbolic execution to model memory-mapped I/O accesses and focus input mutations on values relevant to firmware logic.

papers.title: How Machine Learning Is Solving the Binary Function Similarity Problem
papers.description: Measures binary function similarity research by re-implementing ten representative approaches from the security, programming-language and machine-learning communities in one IDA Pro-based framework, from fuzzy hashing (Catalog1, FunctionSimSearch) to graph neural network, NLP-encoder and transformer models. Two new datasets support six tasks that vary optimization, compiler, bitness and architecture, scored by AUC and ranking metrics, plus a firmware vulnerability-search case. The authors report that fuzzy hashing fails in harder cross-architecture settings, GNN-based models perform best in almost all tasks, and many recent models score similarly on common data.

papers.title: jTrans: Jump-Aware Transformer for Binary Code Similarity Detection
papers.description: jTrans embeds binary functions for similarity search with a BERT-style Transformer. Its jump-aware representation shares parameters between a direct jump’s operand token and the positional embedding of the jump target, so control flow enters the instruction sequence without a separate graph network. The model is pre-trained with masked language modeling and jump-target prediction, then fine-tuned with a cosine triplet objective on functions compiled from the same source at different optimization levels. The paper also introduces BinaryCorp, built by compiling C/C++ packages from Arch Linux’s official repositories and the AUR with gcc and g++.

papers.title: Pop Quiz! Can a Large Language Model Help With Reverse Engineering?
papers.description: Tests whether OpenAI’s Codex model code-davinci-001 can answer reverse-engineering questions about C code in a zero-shot question-and-answer prompt. Programs come from templates the authors wrote, covering cybersecurity snippets and industrial-control algorithms such as PID controllers and filters, plus five single-file Linux malware samples from vx-underground. Each is presented as original or name-randomized source, or as Ghidra decompilation of gcc -O1 builds with debug information, without it, or stripped. After exploratory open-ended questions, generated true/false and short-answer questions about purpose, capabilities and key variables are graded against an answer oracle; Codex answered 72,754 of 136,260 questions correctly.

papers.title: SymLM: Predicting Function Names in Stripped Binaries via Context-Sensitive Execution-Aware Code Embeddings
papers.description: SymLM predicts function names for stripped binaries as sets of name words. It encodes each function’s instructions with a Trex model pretrained on micro-execution traces, fuses them with embeddings of callers, internal callees and external library calls taken from Ghidra’s interprocedural CFG, and scores words from a fixed vocabulary with an MLP decoder; name preprocessing and a word-embedding module, CodeWordNet, handle abbreviations and synonyms. On 1,431,169 functions from 16,027 binaries of 27 projects across x86, x64, ARM and MIPS, O0–O3 and four Hikari obfuscations, the authors report weighted average precision 0.634, recall 0.677 and F1 0.655, plus a firmware case study.

papers.title: The Closer You Look, The More You Learn: A Grey-box Approach to Protocol State Machine Learning
papers.description: StateInspector learns protocol Mealy machines by combining active message queries with snapshots of runtime memory, without requiring the target’s source code. It identifies candidate state-defining heap locations and uses taint and concolic analysis to merge states, evaluated by the authors on TLS 1.2 and WPA/2 implementations.

papers.title: What Your Firmware Tells You Is Not How You Should Emulate It: A Specification-Guided Approach for Firmware Emulation
papers.description: SEmu builds microcontroller peripheral models from vendor reference manuals rather than from the firmware itself. An NLP pipeline built on the Stanford tagger and parser turns register descriptions, interrupt tables and DMA channel tables taken from the manuals into structured condition-action rules, which the emulator checks, executes and chains at run time to answer MMIO accesses and raise interrupts or DMA requests. A symbolic-execution diagnostic tool built on S2E and µEmu traces invalid states back to the rules likely responsible, so that a person can correct them. The authors also use the models for fuzzing and to check driver code against specification rules.

papers.title: Asteria: Deep Learning-based AST-Encoding for Cross-platform Binary Code Similarity Detection
papers.venue: 2021 51st Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks (DSN)
papers.description: ASTERIA uses a Tree-LSTM to encode function ASTs and compare binary functions across platforms. It was evaluated on function pairs and used to search IoT firmware for vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Automatic Firmware Emulation through Invalidity-guided Knowledge Inference
papers.description: µEmu emulates ARM Cortex-M microcontroller firmware without real hardware or hand-written peripheral models by symbolically executing the image with unknown peripheral registers as symbols. Invalidity-guided exploration detects invalid states such as unexpected infinite loops and steers execution toward valid paths, caching the chosen responses at individual peripheral access points in a tiered knowledge base whose rules range from simple storage to PC- and calling-context-based matching. During dynamic analysis the knowledge base answers peripheral reads while an integrated, modified AFL fuzzer supplies data-register input. The prototype extends S2E 2.0 with Cortex-M support.

papers.title: Conware: Automated Modeling of Hardware Peripherals
papers.description: Conware builds reusable software models of hardware peripherals from recordings of real firmware–peripheral interactions. An LLVM pass instruments Arduino source code to log MMIO reads, writes and interrupts on the real board, with existing hardware-in-the-loop recording as an alternative. Each recording becomes a per-peripheral graph whose read values are summarized as simple sub-models such as patterns; graphs are merged and optimized into automata that can be combined across peripherals and run in an Avatar²-based emulator. The authors model ten peripherals on an Arduino Due (SAM3X Cortex-M3) and emulate an uninstrumented smart-door-lock firmware from models trained only on vendor example code.

papers.title: DICE: Automatic Emulation of DMA Input Channels for Dynamic Firmware Analysis
papers.description: DICE adds DMA input emulation to microcontroller firmware emulators that model neither peripherals nor DMA controllers. It watches firmware writes to the memory-mapped DMA controller region for pairs of source and destination transfer pointers, and infers the transfer direction from later firmware accesses. When firmware reads a peripheral-to-RAM destination buffer, DICE answers with analyzer-supplied input such as fuzzer data, growing buffer bounds conservatively. Prototypes patch the QEMU forks of P2IM (ARM Cortex-M) and a PIC32 emulator (MIPS M4K/M-Class). On 83 sample firmware covering 9 DMA controllers from 5 vendors, the authors report 33 of 37 input channels detected with no false positives, correct input for 21 of 22 buffers and 3.4% average overhead. Fuzzing 7 real firmware for 48 hours found 5 previously unknown bugs.

papers.title: ECMO: Peripheral Transplantation to Rehost Embedded Linux Kernels
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2021 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security
papers.description: ECMO transplants peripheral drivers into embedded Linux kernels to boot firmware in QEMU. It evaluated 815 firmware images across 20 kernel versions, 37 device models, and 24 vendors; 710 reached a user-space shell.

papers.title: From Library Portability to Para-rehosting: Natively Executing Microcontroller Software on Commodity Hardware
papers.venue: Proceedings 2021 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
papers.description: The paper uses a POSIX-based portable MCU and replaceable peripheral drivers to rehost MCU software for native execution and security testing on commodity hardware.

papers.title: Jetset: Targeted Firmware Rehosting for Embedded Systems
papers.description: Jetset rehosts firmware only as far as an analyst-chosen goal address, such as the point where a fuzzer can inject input. Given the architecture, the MMIO address range, an entry point and the goal, it symbolically executes the firmware with angr against a modified QEMU, treating peripheral reads as symbolic, cycling interrupts, and steering toward the goal with CFG distances and Tabu search. Solved constraints become C peripheral models for QEMU that replay the inferred values and interrupts so the firmware boots concretely to the goal. The authors evaluate 13 targets across x86, ARM and Motorola ColdFire, including Linux on a Raspberry Pi 2, a BeagleBoard-xM bootloader, a SEL-751 relay, a Boeing 737 CMU-900 and nine P²IM firmware, and use the CMU model with AFL to find a privilege escalation in its VRTX kernel.

papers.title: MappyLand: Fast, Accurate Mapping for Console Games
papers.description: MappyLand, a Rust rewrite of the earlier Mappy system, instruments the FCEUMM NES emulator core to map action/adventure games as they are played from controller inputs. It hooks accesses to the picture-processing unit's scrolling registers and reads emulator memory to register scrolling, separate the playfield from menus, detect and track sprites, build grid-based tile maps and recognize room transitions. An online merging step combines observed rooms into a consistent room graph across backtracking and multiple play sessions. In a 34,514-frame test the authors report about 1.5 ms of mapping overhead per frame, against about 0.2 ms for emulation alone.

papers.title: NetPlier: Probabilistic Network Protocol Reverse Engineering from Message Traces
papers.description: Uses multiple sequence alignment and probabilistic keyword-field inference to cluster network messages by type, evaluated across ten protocols with downstream format and state-machine analysis.

papers.title: Noncompliance as Deviant Behavior: An Automated Black-box Noncompliance Checker for 4G LTE Cellular Devices
papers.description: DIKEUE checks 4G LTE control-plane (NAS and RRC) implementations in commercial phones and modems for noncompliance through differential testing rather than predefined security properties. Its FSM inference module runs TTT active automata learning in LearnLib through an LTE-specific adapter on a modified srsLTE network with a USRP B210 radio, adding a context checker, query cache, inconsistency resolver and reset without rebooting. An equivalence checker then encodes pairs of learned input-output finite state machines for the nuXmv model checker and enumerates diverse deviation-inducing input sequences, which the authors analyze manually.

papers.title: Snipuzz: Black-box Fuzzing of IoT Firmware via Message Snippet Inference
papers.description: Snipuzz fuzzes IoT firmware as a client, using device responses to infer message snippets that guide mutations. It was evaluated on 20 real-world IoT devices and compared with four IoT fuzzing approaches.

papers.title: SoK: Enabling Security Analyses of Embedded Systems via Rehosting
papers.description: Systematizes rehosting: moving embedded firmware from its physical hardware into a virtual environment that models enough hardware behavior for dynamic analysis such as fuzzing and symbolic execution. The authors measure why whole-system emulation does not scale using 2,574 hardware configurations, 1,956 device tree blobs from Linux 5.11.4 and 618 vendor ARM Cortex SVD files. They compare corpus CPU models with QEMU support, count unique peripherals, use driver source lines as a complexity proxy, and run a Monte Carlo simulation of adding peripheral models SoC by SoC. Supporting a random 10% of the SoCs would need about 3,947 peripherals for the Linux corpus and 1,730 for the ARM Cortex corpus, against 1,083 implemented in QEMU 5.2. The paper then classifies prior systems by how they emulate, replace, symbolically model, pass through to hardware or leave each layer unmodified, describes an iterative rehosting process with fidelity evaluation, and sets out open problems.

papers.title: BaseSAFE: Baseband SAnitized Fuzzing through Emulation
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 13th ACM Conference on Security and Privacy in Wireless and Mobile Networks
papers.description: BaseSAFE partially rehosts closed-source cellular baseband firmware for instrumented fuzzing and uses a sanitizing allocator to detect heap buffer overflows.

papers.title: Binary Rewriting without Control Flow Recovery
papers.description: E9Patch statically rewrites x86-64 binaries by inserting jumps to trampolines without moving any other instruction, so the original set of jump targets is preserved and control-flow recovery, symbolization and debug information are not needed. Where a five-byte jump does not fit, instruction punning, padding and successor or neighbor eviction overlap the jump with existing bytes or relocate neighboring instructions into their own trampolines; physical page grouping reduces the memory and file-size cost of scattered trampolines. Instruction locations come from a separate frontend, a basic linear disassembler in the evaluation. The authors evaluate SPEC2006, Ubuntu 16.04 system binaries, and Chrome and Firefox builds over 100 MB, and demonstrate binary repair and heap-write hardening with low fat pointers.

papers.title: BinRec: Dynamic Binary Lifting and Recompilation
papers.description: BinRec lifts an executable to LLVM IR from dynamic traces instead of static disassembly, then lowers the IR back to a recovered binary, so compiler passes can optimize, harden or otherwise transform it. Tracing runs the binary under S²E, which translates the executed code through QEMU into LLVM IR; BinRec removes the emulation instrumentation, merges traces from several inputs into one program, and adds optimizations such as register de-aliasing and promotion of emulated state to locals. When the recovered binary reaches a path that was not traced, a configurable handler stops it, falls back to the original code, or lifts the new path incrementally. The authors report recovering all SPEC CINT2006 benchmarks, including C++ programs, and apply it to reoptimization, control-flow integrity, AddressSanitizer and SafeStack hardening, and partial deobfuscation of virtualization-obfuscated code.

papers.title: Egalito: Layout-Agnostic Binary Recompilation
papers.description: Egalito statically recompiles stripped x86-64 and ARM64 binaries, using the metadata that position-independent executables and libraries carry to recover a complete disassembly in which every code and data cross-reference becomes an explicit link. Its layout-agnostic intermediate representation, EIR, stays close to machine code, so regenerated output is predictable, while a higher-level view supports analysis; data-flow analyses infer jump tables, which have no metadata. Because the original layout imposes no constraints, tools can move or rewrite code freely; the authors build nine, including continuous code randomization in which Egalito transforms itself, a retpoline defense, and software emulation of Intel CET. They report recovering the compiler's jump tables in 866 of 867 executables and libraries from 172 Debian packages, all tests passing in 90 of 149 transformed packages, and a 1.7% speedup on SPEC CPU 2006.

papers.title: FirmAE: Towards Large-Scale Emulation of IoT Firmware for Dynamic Analysis
papers.description: Extends Firmadyne with empirically derived interventions for boot, networking, NVRAM, kernel behavior, and other runtime failures, enabling Linux router and IP-camera firmware web services to run for dynamic analysis.

papers.title: Frankenstein: Advanced Wireless Fuzzing to Exploit New Bluetooth Escalation Targets
papers.description: Frankenstein emulates Bluetooth firmware dumps and fuzzes a virtual modem. It evaluates Broadcom and Cypress stacks, finding three zero-click vulnerabilities, host escalation issues, and BlueFrag on Android.

papers.title: HALucinator: Firmware Re-hosting Through Abstraction Layer Emulation
papers.description: HALucinator rehosts monolithic ARM Cortex-M firmware by identifying hardware-abstraction-library functions and replacing them with authored Python handlers and peripheral models. LibMatch locates library interfaces; the QEMU/Avatar2 implementation supports interactive I/O, while the paper-associated HAL-fuzz variant uses AFL-Unicorn for fuzzing.

papers.title: How far we have come: testing decompilation correctness of C decompilers
papers.description: Tests whether C decompilers preserve program behavior. The authors' DecFuzzer compiles a Csmith-generated program, decompiles the executable, substitutes the decompiled function for the original in the source, recompiles, and compares the two programs' outputs; equivalence-modulo-inputs (EMI) mutation then derives further test programs from the seeds. Across four popular decompilers the authors report 1,423 inputs that trigger decompilation errors and, after manual analysis, 13 bugs in two open-source decompilers. They argue that modern decompilers are making real progress on functional correctness, while type recovery and optimization still hinder accurate output.

papers.title: Learning to Simulate Dynamic Environments with GameGAN
papers.description: GameGAN learns an action-conditioned neural simulator of a game from recorded frames and the actions taken, without access to the game’s logic or engine. An action-conditioned LSTM dynamics engine with a stochastic latent variable predicts the next state, an optional external memory module builds an internal map so that revisited locations stay consistent, and a rendering engine decodes frames while separating static from dynamic components. Training is end-to-end with adversarial losses, including an action-conditioned discriminator, and a temporal cycle loss for memory consistency. The authors evaluate on a modified Pac-Man, a ghost-free Pac-Man-Maze and VizDoom “take cover”, training RL agents inside the learned simulators and testing them in the real games, and measure long-term consistency with a come-back-home task; a human-playable model of the official Pac-Man is shown qualitatively.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Prototyping of Graphical User Interfaces for Mobile Apps
papers.description: ReDraw turns screenshots or design mock-ups into native Android GUI prototypes by detecting components, classifying widget types with a CNN, and assembling a plausible view hierarchy with a data-driven nearest-neighbor method.

papers.title: Neural reverse engineering of stripped binaries using augmented control flow graphs
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA 2020)
papers.description: Nero predicts names for procedures in stripped x86-64 Linux executables; it does not produce decompiled code. Static analysis reconstructs call sites, including imported API names, and augments their arguments with concrete and abstract values along control-flow paths. LSTM, Transformer and graph neural network encoders over the resulting augmented call-site graph feed a decoder that generates the name as subtokens. On a GNU-package test set the authors report 45.53 F1 for Nero-GNN, against 35.52 for an adapted DIRE and 33.66 for Debin.

papers.title: On Manually Reverse Engineering Communication Protocols of Linux Based IoT Systems
papers.description: Presents a manual framework for reverse engineering communication protocols in embedded Linux IoT systems. It applies the framework to several systems and details a WeMo smart plug case study.

papers.title: RetroWrite: Statically Instrumenting COTS Binaries for Fuzzing and Sanitization
papers.description: RetroWrite statically rewrites 64-bit position-independent Linux binaries by generating reassembleable assembly, so instrumentation can be inserted as if at compile time. Instead of heuristics, it symbolizes references from the binary's own metadata: control-flow operands, PC-relative addressing that position-independent code must use, and data relocations become assembler labels, which separates references from scalars. On this base the authors build AFL coverage instrumentation and a binary-only AddressSanitizer. They report fuzzing throughput matching compiler instrumentation and 4.5x faster than AFL's QEMU mode, with more bugs found on LAVA-M, and binary ASan that runs 3x faster than Valgrind memcheck on SPEC CPU2006 and detects 80% more bugs in their evaluation, whose coverage tests use Juliet memory-corruption cases.

papers.title: Towards usable automated detection of CPU architecture and endianness for arbitrary binary files and object code sequences
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Tenth ACM Conference on Data and Application Security and Privacy
papers.description: The paper builds open datasets and tools to identify CPU architecture and endianness in binary files and object code. It evaluates classifiers on executable code sections, reporting over 98% accuracy.

papers.title: Trex: Learning Execution Semantics from Micro-Traces for Binary Similarity
papers.description: Trex learns execution semantics from function micro-traces, then uses that knowledge to match semantically similar binary functions.

papers.title: Automatic Wireless Protocol Reverse Engineering
papers.description: Infers message formats of proprietary wireless protocols from demodulated physical-layer captures: it aligns messages by preamble and sync word, then uses RSSI and dedicated engines to label length, address, sequence-number and checksum fields, optionally using known addresses or field positions.

papers.title: Coda: An End-to-End Neural Program Decompiler
papers.description: Coda decompiles the assembly of short functions into C in two phases. An instruction-type-aware N-ary Tree-LSTM encoder and an attention-fed AST decoder first generate a code sketch; an ensemble of neural error predictors then proposes token corrections, each kept only if recompiling the candidate does not increase its edit distance to the input assembly. On synthetic benchmarks the authors report 82% average program accuracy after correction, against 12% for a sequence-to-sequence baseline with attention.

papers.title: DIRE: A Neural Approach to Decompiled Identifier Naming
papers.description: Combines lexical and structural information from decompiler output to predict meaningful variable names, with a training and evaluation corpus derived from compiled C projects.

papers.title: ICSREF: A Framework for Automated Reverse Engineering of Industrial Control Systems Binaries
papers.venue: Proceedings 2019 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
papers.description: ICSREF automates reverse engineering of PLC binaries compiled with CODESYS. It was evaluated on collected and in-house PLC binaries and used to generate an attack against a chemical process testbed.

papers.title: InternalBlue - Bluetooth Binary Patching and Experimentation Framework
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Annual International Conference on Mobile Systems, Applications, and Services
papers.description: The paper reverse engineers Broadcom Bluetooth controllers and presents InternalBlue for patching their firmware. It evaluates the framework through vulnerability tests, bug fixes, and added security features.

papers.title: LibreCAN: Automated CAN Message Translator
papers.description: LibreCAN reverse-engineers proprietary CAN message formats from traffic recorded at a vehicle's OBD-II port, without the OEM's DBC translation files. Phase 0 extracts candidate signal boundaries from bit-flip behaviour, extending the earlier READ algorithm; Phase 1 correlates extracted signals with standard OBD-II PIDs and smartphone IMU data to identify kinematic signals and estimate their scale and offset; Phase 2 filters the CAN IDs recorded while a driver performs 53 scripted body-related events to shortlist candidate IDs for each event.

papers.title: Manticore: A User-Friendly Symbolic Execution Framework for Binaries and Smart Contracts
papers.description: Manticore uses dynamic symbolic execution to analyze binaries and Ethereum smart contracts. The paper presents its architecture and demonstrates bug finding and code verification used for commercial clients.

papers.title: Towards Neural Decompilation
papers.description: The paper trains a neural machine translation decompiler using a compiler. It evaluates translation from LLVM IR and x86 assembly to C, successfully decompiling over 97% and 88% of its respective benchmarks.

papers.title: A Cross-Architecture Instruction Embedding Model for Natural Language Processing-Inspired Binary Code Analysis
papers.description: The paper learns instruction embeddings that capture semantic relationships within and across architectures. It evaluates them on semantic basic-block comparison, outperforming a code-statistics approach.

papers.title: Debin: Predicting Debug Information in Stripped Binaries
papers.description: Debin predicts debug information for stripped ELF binaries on x86, x64 and ARM. After lifting code to BAP-IR, an Extremely randomized Trees classifier decides which registers and memory offsets hold source-level variables. A conditional random field, solved with Nice2Predict, then jointly predicts names and types for variables and functions, and the result is written back as DWARF sections. On 300 held-out binaries per architecture, the authors report 68.8% precision and 68.3% recall for x64 names and types.

papers.title: From UI Design Image to GUI Skeleton: A Neural Machine Translator to Bootstrap Mobile GUI Implementation
papers.description: UI2code translates a mobile UI image into an Android component hierarchy and layout skeleton using a neural encoder-decoder. The paper evaluates structural prediction and a small developer study of implementing layouts from generated skeletons.

papers.title: NEMESYS: Network Message Syntax Reverse Engineering by Analysis of the Intrinsic Structure of Individual Messages
papers.description: Infers approximate field boundaries within individual binary-protocol messages from changes in bit congruence, and introduces Format Match Score to compare inferred segmentation with known protocol dissectors.

papers.title: pix2code: Generating Code from a Graphical User Interface Screenshot
papers.description: Learns screenshot-to-DSL generation for native Android XML, iOS Storyboards and web HTML/CSS interfaces, then compiles the DSL into platform UI code.

papers.title: Game Engine Learning from Video
papers.description: Learns a rule-based forward simulator of a 2D game from gameplay video. Using a supplied sprite palette, OpenCV locates sprites in each frame; matched sprites are converted into hand-designed fact types for animation, position, relative distance, x and y velocity and camera offset. Game Engine Search then scans the frames, and whenever the current engine’s predicted next frame differs from the real one by more than a threshold, it runs a greedy search over engines that add or modify condition–effect rules or mark them as player-controlled. Engines are ranked by pixel error and rule count. Trained on one Super Mario Bros. Level 1-1 video, the learned engine predicts frames of a different player’s video more accurately than a CNN frame predictor and a previous-frame baseline, and a value-iteration agent planning with it shows no significant difference from one using the Infinite Mario engine’s native forward simulation.

papers.title: Mechanics Automatically Recognized via Interactive Observation: Jumping
papers.description: Infers platform-game jump mechanics by running controlled experiments in a modified FCEUX NES emulator. A person first plays each game to a safe state; the system then repeatedly holds the jump button for 1 to 120 frames, waits 120 frames and resets, recording every sprite from the PPU sprite table. Sprites that usually touch one another are merged into characters and tracked. A hand-designed four-state jump automaton (ground, rising with and without the button, falling) is then fitted with linear support vector regression, giving per-state velocity and gravity parameters plus minimum and maximum button-hold durations. Across 48 games (about 30% of NES platformers) and 52 characters, the authors cluster the learned jumps into three styles.

papers.title: Ramblr: Making Reassembly Great Again
papers.description: Ramblr produces reassembleable disassembly: assembly recovered from a stripped binary that can be edited and assembled again with an off-the-shelf assembler. Starting from angr's CFG recovery, it classifies the contents of data regions, then decides which immediates and data values are references to code or data that must become symbols. Base-pointer reattribution handles compiler-optimized references that point outside their target object, and sanity checks let Ramblr refuse to reassemble a binary it cannot handle safely, such as one that encrypts pointers. The authors evaluate 106 GNU Coreutils programs for x86 and x86-64 and 143 DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge binaries at six optimization levels. They report that Uroboros broke 22.64% of 32-bit Coreutils binaries at -O0 and 56.61% at -O1, while Ramblr broke none, and that Ramblr reassembled over 98% of CGC binaries at every level.

papers.title: rev.ng: A Unified Binary Analysis Framework to Recover CFGs and Function Boundaries
papers.description: rev.ng lifts binaries to LLVM IR through QEMU's tiny code generator, so one front end covers every architecture QEMU supports and the output is compilable IR. On that IR the authors build architecture-independent analyses that recover a program's control-flow graph and function boundaries without symbols or debugging information. A value-range analysis (OSRA) bounds indirect jump targets such as switch tables, and further analyses handle predicated instructions, noreturn functions, tail calls and context-dependent control flow. On coreutils built for MIPS, ARM and x86-64 with GCC and clang at -O2, -O3 and -Os, its function-boundary accuracy is close to IDA Pro and better than BAP/ByteWeight and angr.

papers.title: Rico: A Mobile App Dataset for Building Data-Driven Design Applications
papers.description: Rico is a dataset of Android app designs and a runtime mining system that needs no access to or modification of app source code. Crowd workers used free Google Play apps through a web interface to a device farm, recording interaction traces. An automated crawler then replayed each trace and kept exploring, using a screenshot-and-resource-id similarity heuristic to identify new UI states. The paper reports 10,811 traces and 72,219 unique UIs from 9,772 apps in 27 categories. Each UI has a screenshot, augmented view hierarchy, explored interactions, transition animations and a 64-dimensional autoencoder layout vector.

papers.title: Statistical Deobfuscation of Android Applications
papers.description: DeGuard reverses layout obfuscation in Android APKs, predicting original names for the fields, methods, classes and packages that ProGuard renames. Built on Soot, it represents an app as a dependency graph over program elements and keeps Android API and other unobfuscated names fixed. It then runs MAP inference with Nice2Predict on a conditional random field learned from 1,684 F-Droid apps, under constraints that keep the renamed APK semantically equivalent. On 100 held-out F-Droid apps obfuscated with ProGuard, names identical to the originals rise from 13.3% to 79.1%, and third-party library prediction reaches 91.3% precision and 91.0% recall.

papers.title: Towards Automated Dynamic Analysis for Linux-based Embedded Firmware
papers.description: Firmadyne crawls, extracts and emulates Linux-based firmware for network-connected commercial devices such as routers and IP cameras. It replaces the vendor kernel with pre-built, instrumented kernels for little-endian ARM and little- and big-endian MIPS, boots the extracted filesystem under QEMU full-system emulation with a userspace NVRAM library, infers the network configuration, then runs automated analyses including 60 known and 14 newly found exploits. From 23,035 images across 42 vendors, the authors extracted 9,486 and report 887 of the 1,971 network-reachable images vulnerable to at least one sampled exploit.

papers.title: Automated Dynamic Firmware Analysis at Scale: A Case Study on Embedded Web Interfaces
papers.description: The paper emulates firmware images and uses static and dynamic tools to find vulnerabilities in embedded web interfaces. It evaluated 1,925 images from 54 vendors and found vulnerabilities in 185 images.

papers.title: No More Gotos: Decompilation Using Pattern-Independent Control-Flow Structuring and Semantics-Preserving Transformations
papers.description: DREAM is a decompiler whose control-flow structuring recovers loops, conditionals and switch statements from a recovered control-flow graph without matching predefined region patterns. For acyclic regions it computes each node's reaching condition, then refines the resulting conditions into if-then-else and switch constructs; cyclic regions are structured as loops whose type and continuation condition are inferred. Semantics-preserving transformations first rewrite cyclic regions with multiple entries or successors into single-entry, single-successor regions, and a Boolean variable keeps a repeated test equivalent when its operands may change. On GNU coreutils the authors report no goto statements, against thousands from Hex-Rays and Phoenix, and more compact code than Hex-Rays for 72.7% of functions and than Phoenix for 98.8% in one-to-one comparisons.

papers.title: Reverse Engineering Mobile Application User Interfaces with REMAUI (T)
papers.description: Reconstructs native Android UI code from screenshots or design bitmaps using OCR, computer vision, and layout heuristics; evaluates visual similarity and view hierarchies on 488 screenshots from over 100 Android and iOS applications.

papers.title: Avatar: A Framework to Support Dynamic Security Analysis of Embedded Systems’ Firmwares
papers.description: Avatar runs embedded firmware in an instrumented emulator, S²E on QEMU, while forwarding memory-mapped I/O to the real device and injecting the device's interrupts back into the emulator, so firmware that depends on undocumented peripherals can still be analyzed dynamically. The device is reached through JTAG via OpenOCD or through a small debugging stub over a serial line. Because forwarding every access over a 38400-baud serial link is very slow, about five instructions per second in one of the authors' measurements, Avatar also keeps memory that never behaves like I/O local to the emulator, migrates selected code to run natively on the device, and switches state between the two. With S²E's selective symbolic execution, the authors probe a hard-disk mask-ROM bootloader for hidden commands, an IEEE 802.15.4 sensor node for an injected overflow, and the SMS decoding routines of a GSM feature phone.

papers.title: Towards Automated Protocol Reverse Engineering Using Semantic Information
papers.description: Infers the vocabulary of an undocumented protocol, its message types and formats, from communication traces. The approach uses contextual information embedded in the messages to improve message clustering and the identification of field boundaries; the HAL record lists contextual clustering and semantic sequence alignment as keywords. The authors motivate the work with parsers and traffic generators for network security products, and compare it with their own reimplementations of ASAP, Discoverer and ScriptGen. The first two authors are the authors of Netzob, the open-source protocol reverse-engineering framework.

papers.title: Understanding JavaScript Event-Based Interactions
papers.description: Clematis helps developers understand a JavaScript web application's runtime behavior from a recorded user session. A proxy instruments JavaScript on the fly to log DOM events, timeouts, XMLHttpRequest phases, function calls and DOM mutations. The trace is grouped into episodes, each with its triggering event, executed functions and resulting DOM changes, linked by temporal and causal edges and shown in an interactive visualization. In an industrial study with 20 developers on the Phormer photo gallery, the authors report 61% higher task accuracy and 47% less completion time than developers using their preferred tools.

papers.title: Guided GUI Testing of Android Apps with Minimal Restart and Approximate Learning
papers.description: SwiftHand generates test inputs for Android apps while learning an approximate GUI model during testing. It instruments Dalvik bytecode to read the GUI component tree and derive each screen's enabled touch, scroll, text, Back and Menu inputs; screens with the same enabled inputs are treated as equivalent states of an extended deterministic labeled transition system. The learned model steers execution toward unexplored frontier states and avoids restarts, since reinstalling an app took about 30 seconds. On 10 F-Droid apps, the authors report higher branch coverage than random and L*-based testing within the time budget, reached faster.

papers.title: Crawling Ajax-Based Web Applications through Dynamic Analysis of User Interface State Changes
papers.description: Crawljax infers a state-flow graph of an Ajax web application by driving it in a real browser. It scans the DOM for candidate clickable elements, fires events on them, compares the resulting DOM against known states with configurable comparison and similarity thresholds, and records new states and the event transitions between them, backtracking by reloading and replaying paths. A concurrent variant partitions the crawl across browser instances. The Java tool uses Selenium WebDriver and plugins; one plugin writes a static mirror of the crawled states. The authors evaluate six open-source and industrial sites and measure how the number of concurrent browsers affects crawling runtime on Google AdSense.

papers.title: Prospex: Protocol Specification Extraction
papers.description: Prospex infers message formats and a protocol state machine from execution traces of a Linux server handling client sessions. Dynamic taint analysis splits each session into messages and recovers their formats; messages are then clustered into types by input-format, execution and server-impact similarity, such as the system calls, outputs and file paths a message triggers. The observed type sequences form an augmented prefix tree acceptor, which prerequisite and end-state heuristics label before Exbar computes a minimal consistent automaton. The resulting specifications are translated for the Peach fuzzer to reach later protocol states. The evaluation covers the Agobot command-and-control protocol, SMTP on Sendmail, SMB on Samba and SIP on Asterisk.

papers.title: Tupni: Automatic Reverse Engineering of Input Formats
papers.description: Tupni infers an input format from an execution trace of an x86 program parsing one input, using byte-level dynamic taint tracking. It segments the input into fields from the instructions that operate on tainted bytes, finds record sequences from parsing loops, groups records into types by the code that handles them, and emits an enhanced BNF grammar with length, value and some inter-message constraints. Grammars from several inputs can be merged into a more complete specification. The evaluation covers five file formats (WMF, BMP, JPG, PNG, TIF) and five network protocols (DNS, RPC, TFTP, HTTP, FTP), and the output is used for zero-day vulnerability signature generation with ShieldGen.

papers.title: Polyglot: Automatic Extraction of Protocol Message Format using Dynamic Binary Analysis
papers.description: Polyglot infers the format of a message that a program receives by monitoring how the program binary processes it, an approach the authors call shadowing. An execution monitor taints network input and records an instruction trace; offline analyses then find direction fields, such as length and pointer fields, from tainted memory accesses and loop conditions, separators from comparisons between tainted bytes and constants, multi-byte fixed-length fields from how instructions group input bytes, and protocol keywords from successful comparisons. It works on stripped IA-32 binaries without source code or debugging information.

papers.title: GUI ripping: reverse engineering of graphical user interfaces for testing
papers.description: GUI ripping reverse engineers a test model from a running desktop application rather than from its source code or specifications. Starting from the top-level windows, a ripper opens each child window by programmatically clicking executable widgets, records every window’s widgets, properties and values, and builds a GUI forest of windows. From that forest it derives event-flow graphs, which record which events can follow one another within a component, and an integration tree of component invocations. The paper describes rippers for Microsoft Windows applications, using window handles and the Windows API, and for Java Swing applications, using Java’s AWT and Swing APIs. It applies them to WordPad, Notepad, Yahoo Messenger and four applications of the TerpOffice student office suite, with the models feeding automated test generation in the authors’ GUITAR and DART systems.
